The words

Lord, who at Cana's wedding feast
Didst as a Guest appear,
Thou dearer far than earthly guest,
Vouchsafe Thy presence here.
For holy Thou indeed dost prove
The marriage vow to be,
Proclaiming it a type of love
Between the Church and Thee.

The holiest vow that man can make,
The golden thread in life,
The bond that none may dare to break,
That bindeth man and wife,
Which, blest by Thee, whate'er betide,
No evil shall destroy,
Through careworn days each care divides
And doubles every joy.

On those who at Thine altar kneel,
O Lord, Thy blessing pour,
That each may wake the other's zeal
To love Thee more and more.
Oh, grant them here in peace to live,
In purity and love,
And, this world leaving, to receive
A crown of life above.

How to sing it from the solfa

  • Find doh first. Play or hum G and sing d r m f s up from it, so the whole choir has the key in their ears before you start.
  • Pitch the first note. The tune starts on m (B), on the word “Lord”, as a pickup before the first full bar.
  • Count the time. 4/4 means four crotchet beats in each bar. In the grid every cell is half a crotchet: a dash (–) holds the note before it, and _ is a rest.
  • Know the notes. The tune uses d r m f s l t and the chromatic fe. A comma after a note (s,) is the octave below; an apostrophe (d') is the octave above.

About the hymn

The words are by Adelaide Thrupp, first published in 1853. The tune, ST. URSULA, is by Frederick Westlake (1863). This version of the melody and the words comes from the Open Hymnal Project.

  • Words (1853): Adelaide Thrupp (1831–1908)
  • Music (1863): Frederick Westlake (1840–1898)

Melody and words from the Open Hymnal Project (public domain), edited by Brian J. Dumont; tune ST. URSULA by Frederick Westlake (1840–1898); words by Adelaide Thrupp (1831–1908). Questions about Lord, Who at Cana's Wedding Feast

What is the doh of Lord, Who at Cana's Wedding Feast?

In this version, in G major, doh is G. If your choir sings it in another key, doh moves to the new key note and every solfa syllable stays the same — that is what movable doh means.

What note does Lord, Who at Cana's Wedding Feast start on?

It starts on m (B in G major), a pickup on the word “Lord” before the first full bar. Find doh first, then sing up or down to m.

Is Lord, Who at Cana's Wedding Feast in the public domain?

Yes. Adelaide Thrupp died in 1908, Frederick Westlake died in 1898; the words were first published in 1853 and the music in 1863. Everyone named died before 1955 and both were published before 1929, so the hymn is out of copyright in the UK, the EU, the United States and Nigeria. Modern arrangements and translations can still be under copyright.
